introduction_markdown: Duration: Three Hours. Answer BOTH questions in SECTION A and ONE EACH from SECTIONS B and C in the SAME Answer Booklet, beginning each section on a new page. Read all instructions on BOTH the question paper and the answer booklet very carefully. Failure to obey these instructions or to number your work as on the question paper will cause you to lose marks. Any unusual mark, sign or unnecessary disclosure of your identity will be considered as an attempt to cheat and will earn you a penalty. In the SUMMARY question, use mainly your own words. Indiscriminate copying of portions of the passage as your answer will earn you little or no marks. You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers. A pre-prepared or memorised composition will earn you little or no marks.
enonce_intro_markdown:
**SECTION C: PRESCRIBED TEXTS (20 marks)**

Answer ONE question only.

**1.** Read the following extract from John N. Nkengasong's *Across the Mongolo* and answer the questions below it.

(L1) Nwolefeck returned too soon. The Chief and the Doctor lowered their voices as he sat down and chatted with me. I  
(L2) wished he had delayed a little longer so that I could follow to the end the conversation between the Chief and the  
(L3) Doctor. That was the truth. The younger generation had to do something. It is not because the *old men have lost their*  
(L4) *teeth* that the young men will not eat the bones. Something had to be done. It was clearly the place of the younger  
(L5) generation to raise their voices and ask for their rights. *Their future had been auctioned* and it was they who ought to  
(L6) fight hard to retrieve it. Their elders were *limping to their graves* with their guilt. However, how was that to save the  
(L7) situation? It was clearly the place of those whose future had been auctioned to act, those whose destiny had been  
(L8) auctioned *in exchange for inconsequential political posts* to act.

questions.enonce_markdown: **a.** Briefly recount what precedes this scene. (4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Method answer: model of the structure (corrigé de méthode : the novel itself is not available)**

What the extract itself lets us say about the moment before it:

- The narrator is present while the Chief and the Doctor hold a private conversation about the situation of the younger generation; he wants to follow it "to the end", so it was important and serious.
- Nwolefeck then comes back "too soon" and sits down to chat, so the Chief and the Doctor lower their voices and the narrator loses the end of their talk.
- From the narrator's own thoughts, the conversation concerned how the elders have failed the young people and the need for the young to act and claim their rights.

How to earn the 4 marks: write four or five clear sentences in the PAST tense, in order, naming the characters (the narrator, the Chief, the Doctor, Nwolefeck), the place and the subject of the talk, and what led the narrator to be listening. Do not retell the whole story and do not add details that the novel does not contain. A candidate who has read the novel gives the events of the preceding chapter (the exact cause and setting of the conversation), which must come from the book.

| Marks | What earns them |
|---|---|
| 2 | The correct setting and the characters present |
| 2 | The correct subject of the conversation and the immediate lead-up, in order and in the past tense |

questions.enonce_markdown:
**b.** Give the meaning in context of the following expressions:

i "... old men have lost their teeth." (L3)

ii "...their future had been auctioned" (L5)

iii ".... limping to their graves" (L6)

iv "...in exchange for inconsequential political posts" (L7-8) (4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
One mark for each expression: the meaning must fit the context, not be a dictionary definition.

| Expression | Meaning in context |
|---|---|
| i "old men have lost their teeth" (L3) | The elders are now weak and powerless, like toothless old people who can no longer bite; but the narrator says that this is no reason why the young should go hungry ("not eat the bones"): the young must act in spite of the weakness of the old. |
| ii "their future had been auctioned" (L5) | The young people's future has been sold off like goods at a public sale: others, the leaders of the older generation, have bargained it away without consulting them, for their own profit. |
| iii "limping to their graves" (L6) | The elders are close to the end of life, moving slowly and painfully towards death, weighed down by the guilt of what they have done; they are too weak and too late to put things right. |
| iv "in exchange for inconsequential political posts" (L7-8) | In return for unimportant positions in politics, without any real power: the leaders gave away the destiny of the young for a very small reward. |
themes: A Level English - vocabulary in context
A Level English - idioms and proverbs

questions.enonce_markdown: **c.** Comment on the effective use of any two metaphorical expressions in the extract. (2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Choose two and give for each: the expression, what it is compared with, and the effect (1 mark each).

1. **"their future had been auctioned" (L5)**: the future is compared with an object sold in an auction. The image is effective because it makes the betrayal concrete and shameful: the young people's destiny has been put on sale and sold to the highest bidder, without their consent, which stirs anger and a sense of injustice.
2. **"limping to their graves" (L6)**: the elders are compared with an injured person walking painfully. The image is effective because it shows their weakness, their closeness to death and the burden of their guilt in one picture; it makes them pitiful and useless as defenders of the young.

(Also acceptable: "old men have lost their teeth" and "will not eat the bones", an image of weakness and hunger, which pushes the young to act.)
themes: A Level English - figures of speech

questions.enonce_markdown: **d.** Pick four different adverbs from the extract and say what type they are. (4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
One mark for each adverb correctly picked and identified. Four different types are best:

| Adverb | Line | Type | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| soon | L1 ("returned too soon") | adverb of time | answers "when?" |
| hard | L6 ("fight hard") | adverb of manner | answers "how?" |
| too | L1 ("too soon") | adverb of degree | modifies the adverb "soon" |
| However | L6 | conjunctive adverb (linking adverb) | joins the sentence to the preceding one and expresses contrast |

Other correct choices: "clearly" (L4, L7; adverb of manner or of attitude, giving the narrator's view), "longer" (L2; adverb of time or duration, comparative), "little" in "a little longer" (adverb of degree), "how" (L6; interrogative adverb of manner), "not" (L4; adverb of negation). Do not accept "so" in "so that" (a conjunction).
themes: A Level English - parts of speech

questions.enonce_markdown: **e.** What is the major concern in the extract? Show how this concern is raised and treated in any two other prescribed texts. (6 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Method answer (corrigé de méthode : the other prescribed texts are not available)**

**The concern in the extract (about 2 marks, established by the passage).** The major concern is the betrayal of the younger generation by the older leaders, who have "auctioned" the young people's future for "inconsequential political posts"; linked to it are the powerlessness and guilt of the elders and the duty of the young to "raise their voices", claim their rights and act.

**Treatment in two other prescribed texts (about 4 marks, 2 for each text).** For each of two texts chosen from the syllabus list, write one short paragraph with this structure:

1. Name the text and the author, and say how the concern appears (a character who sells out others for personal gain, leaders who ignore the young, a struggle between generations, corruption, a call for change).
2. Give a precise example from the text (an episode, a character, a short quotation) that the candidate knows well.
3. Say how the writer treats it (tone, point of view, outcome: the young succeed, fail, or are warned; irony, satire, sympathy).
4. Link back to the extract in one phrase.

Use a short introduction (the concern) and a short conclusion. The examples must come from the texts the candidate has studied, and only from them.
themes: A Level English - tone and attitude
